app_description: Earthquakes around the world, as they happen.
truncated_notice: Showing only the {limit} most recent, in the table and on the map. Narrow the dates or the area to see the rest.
place_search_error: Place search is unavailable right now. You can still use your location.
timeline_histogram_hint: Use the arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, Home and End to move the playback window.
crustal_block_explainer_what: A 3D cut of the ground around the Epicenter. Its colors show the layers CRUST1.0, a global model of the Earth's crust, estimates here.
crustal_block_explainer_crust: The crust is the Earth's thin rocky skin: about 5–10 km thick under the oceans and 30–70 km under the continents. Underneath lies the mantle, hot rock that flows very slowly. The boundary between the two is called the Moho.
crustal_block_explainer_depth: The white dot marks where the rupture started. The shallower it starts, the closer its energy is to the surface and the harder the ground above usually shakes. Deep earthquakes are felt more gently, but over a wider area.
crustal_block_explainer_relief: Mountains and sea floors are drawn 10 times taller than they really are so you can see them. The layers underneath are drawn to scale.
crustal_block_no_webgl: The 3D view isn't available on this device. The layers are listed below.
crustal_block_error: Couldn't load the layers under the Epicenter.
crustal_block_attribution_crust: CRUST1.0 — Laske, G., Masters, G., Ma, Z. & Pasyanos, M. (2013)
crustal_block_attribution_terrain: Terrain Tiles (Mapzen/Tilezen, AWS Open Data): ETOPO1 © NOAA, SRTM and GMTED2010 © USGS, EU-DEM © Copernicus and other sources
crustal_block_explain_water: Ocean or sea water above the sea floor. It isn't rock, but CRUST1.0 counts it as the top layer.
crustal_block_explain_ice: Permanent ice, such as an ice sheet or a glacier, resting on the rock.
crustal_block_explain_upper_sediments: Loose, young sediment: sand, mud and the remains of sea life, laid down on top of the rock.
crustal_block_explain_middle_sediments: Older sediment, pressed by the weight above until it starts to turn into rock.
crustal_block_explain_lower_sediments: The oldest, most compacted sediment, by now mostly solid sedimentary rock.
crustal_block_explain_upper_crust: Solid rock, mostly granite-like under the continents. Most earthquakes start in this layer, where the rock is cold and stiff enough to snap.
crustal_block_explain_middle_crust: Denser rock, hotter and under more pressure than the layer above.
crustal_block_explain_lower_crust: The deepest, densest part of the crust, often basalt-like rock, resting on the mantle.
crustal_block_explain_moho: The boundary between the crust and the mantle. Earthquake waves suddenly speed up when they cross it, which is how Andrija Mohorovičić discovered it in 1909.
crustal_block_explain_upper_mantle: Hot, dense rock that is solid but creeps a few centimeters a year. The tectonic plates move on top of it.
crustal_block_explain_transition_zone: At about 400 km the pressure is so great that the mantle's minerals rearrange into denser forms. The deepest earthquakes happen in this zone.
crustal_block_explain_lower_mantle: From about 670 km the minerals squeeze into even denser forms. No earthquake has been recorded starting much deeper than this.
crustal_block_explain_rupture_start: Where the rupture began, straight below the Epicenter. Shallow ruptures, in the top few tens of kilometers, shake the surface above them hardest. Deeper ones lose energy on the way up, so they are felt more gently but over a wider area.
detail_not_found_body: The agency has no Earthquake with this ID. The link may be mistyped, or the Earthquake may have been removed.
detail_train_usgs_real: Real: the shape and colour of each line are the USGS ShakeMap isoseismals, lines joining places with the same estimated intensity.
detail_train_usgs_recreated: Recreated: the moving front. It advances at a steady pace, like the S wave sped up, its shape between two isoseismals is interpolated, and it loops. It does not show when the shaking reached each place.
detail_train_emsc_real: Real: each bubble groups felt reports sent to EMSC, coloured by their average intensity.
detail_train_circle_recreated: Recreated: the rings. They are S-wave fronts, sped up and looped, that fade out where the app estimates the shaking stops being felt (intensity II), from magnitude and depth only.
detail_train_reports_recreated: Recreated: the rings. They are S-wave fronts, sped up and looped, that reach the farthest place where someone reported feeling it.
detail_facts_explainer_magnitude: Magnitude measures the energy released where the ground broke. Each whole step up is about 32 times more energy, so a magnitude 7 releases roughly 1,000 times more than a magnitude 5.
detail_facts_explainer_intensity: Magnitude is not how hard the ground shakes where you are. That is Intensity, and it is strongest near the Epicenter and fades with distance.
detail_depth_explain: How far below the surface the rupture started. Shallow Earthquakes (under about 70 km) usually shake the ground harder than deep ones of the same magnitude.
detail_epicenter_explain: The point on the surface directly above where the rupture started, as latitude and longitude. N and S mean north and south of the equator; E and W mean east and west of the Greenwich meridian.
detail_significance_explain: A single USGS score, from 0 to over 1,000, that combines magnitude, how many people felt it and the estimated impact. Higher scores mean USGS considers the Earthquake more significant.
detail_status_explain: Reviewed means a seismologist checked and corrected the automatic result. Automatic results come first, within minutes, and can change.
detail_magtype_mww: Moment magnitude computed from the W-phase, a slow wave that arrives after the first waves. It is the most reliable measure for large Earthquakes.
detail_magtype_mwc: Moment magnitude from a centroid moment tensor, which models the whole rupture instead of one wave. Reliable for moderate and large Earthquakes.
detail_magtype_mwb: Moment magnitude computed from body waves, the waves that travel through the Earth's interior.
detail_magtype_mwr: Moment magnitude computed from the full recorded waveforms at regional stations.
detail_magtype_mw: Moment magnitude, based on the size of the rupture and how far the rock slipped. It does not saturate, so it works for the largest Earthquakes.
detail_magtype_mb: Body-wave magnitude, measured from the first waves that travel through the Earth. Good for moderate Earthquakes, but it underestimates the largest ones.
detail_magtype_ml: Local magnitude, the original Richter scale, measured from nearby seismometers. Best for small, close Earthquakes.
detail_magtype_md: Duration magnitude, estimated from how long the shaking lasts on a seismogram. Used mostly for small Earthquakes.
detail_magtype_ms: Surface-wave magnitude, measured from the slow waves that travel along the Earth's surface. Suited to shallow, moderate to large Earthquakes.
detail_magtype_other: The method used to calculate the magnitude. Different methods suit different sizes and distances, so the same Earthquake can get slightly different values.
detail_fault_strike_slip_explain: The two sides of the fault slid past each other horizontally, like two cars passing in opposite lanes.
detail_fault_normal_explain: The ground on one side of the fault dropped down relative to the other, as the crust was being stretched apart.
detail_fault_reverse_explain: The ground on one side of the fault was pushed up and over the other, as the crust was being squeezed together.
detail_fault_oblique_normal_explain: A mix of sliding sideways and dropping down, with the dropping down dominating.
detail_fault_oblique_reverse_explain: A mix of sliding sideways and being pushed up, with the pushing up dominating.
detail_origin_explainer_what: Seismologists find where an Earthquake started by timing when its waves reach each seismometer. These figures show how that location was calculated and how much to trust it.
detail_origin_explainer_how: In general, more stations, a smaller gap between them and smaller errors mean a better located Earthquake.
detail_depth_type_explain: How the depth was determined. Depth is the hardest part of the location to pin down.
detail_depth_type_location: Calculated from the wave arrival times
detail_horizontal_error_explain: The uncertainty of the Epicenter. The true position is probably within this distance of the point shown.
detail_vertical_error_explain: The uncertainty of the depth. The true depth is probably within this many kilometers above or below the value shown.
detail_azimuthal_gap_explain: The largest angle around the Epicenter with no station. Picture looking at the Earthquake from above: a smaller gap means stations surround it, and the location is better. Under 180° is generally good.
detail_stations_explain: How many seismometers recorded this Earthquake and were used to locate it. More stations make the location more reliable.
detail_phases_explain: How many individual wave arrival times were used. Each station can contribute several, such as the first and second waves.
detail_standard_error_explain: On average, how many seconds the observed arrival times differ from the ones the location predicts. Smaller means the data fit the result better.
detail_minimum_distance_explain: Distance to the closest station, in degrees of arc on the Earth. One degree is about 111 km. A close station pins the depth down better.
detail_review_status_explain: Whether a seismologist reviewed this location or it is still the automatic result.
detail_network_explain: The code of the seismic network that contributed this location. For example, US is the USGS National Earthquake Information Center.
detail_impact_explainer_what: Estimates of how strongly the ground shook and how serious the consequences may be, built by USGS from models and from reports by the public.
detail_impact_explainer_intensity: Shaking is described with Intensity, from I (not felt) to X (extreme). Unlike magnitude, Intensity is different at every place: it depends on the distance, the ground and the buildings.
detail_pager_explain: A USGS estimate of how many people may have died and how much economic damage there may be, shown as a traffic-light color.
detail_pager_green_explain: Green means few or no fatalities and little damage are expected.
detail_pager_yellow_explain: Yellow means some casualties and damage are possible, and a local response is likely enough.
detail_pager_orange_explain: Orange means significant casualties and damage are likely, and a regional response may be needed.
detail_pager_red_explain: Red means high casualties and damage are likely, and a national or international response may be needed.
detail_shakemap_explain: The highest Intensity estimated anywhere, from a map that combines sensor readings and models. Intensity VI is strong enough to cause light damage; VIII and above damages ordinary buildings.
detail_dyfi_responses_explain: How many people answered the USGS online survey about what they felt. More reports mean a better picture of the shaking.
detail_dyfi_intensity_explain: The highest Intensity that people reported in their answers. It can differ from the ShakeMap, which is based on sensors and models.
detail_tsunami_explain: USGS marks large Earthquakes under or near the ocean. It only says a tsunami was possible; it is not a tsunami warning. For warnings and instructions, follow the official tsunami warning centers and local authorities.
detail_mechanism_explainer_what: The focal mechanism describes how the rock moved during the Earthquake: which way the fault is tilted and in which direction each side slid.
detail_mechanism_explainer_beachball: The “beach ball” is the Earth seen from above at the point where the rupture started. Dark quadrants are where the first wave pushed away from the source (compression); white quadrants are where it pulled toward it.
detail_mechanism_explainer_planes: The pattern fits two possible fault planes at right angles. The data alone cannot tell which one actually broke, so both are listed.
detail_beachball_title: Beach ball diagram of the focal mechanism
detail_beachball_caption: Dark areas: compression. White areas: pulling toward the source.
detail_strike_explain: The compass direction of the fault line on the surface, in degrees from north (0° to 360°).
detail_dip_explain: How steeply the fault plane tilts down from horizontal. 0° is flat, 90° is vertical.
detail_rake_explain: The direction the rock slid along the fault, measured on the fault plane. Near 0° or 180° is sideways, positive means pushed up, negative means dropped down.
detail_double_couple_explain: How much of the rupture fits a simple slip on a fault. Close to 100% means a clean fault slip; lower values suggest a more complex rupture.
detail_scalar_moment_explain: A physical measure of the Earthquake's size, in newton-meters: the area that broke, times the slip, times the rock's stiffness. Moment magnitude is calculated from it.
detail_derived_magnitude_explain: The magnitude calculated from this focal mechanism. It can differ slightly from the headline magnitude.
detail_derived_depth_explain: The depth that best fits this focal mechanism. It can differ from the location depth, since it comes from a different calculation.
detail_emsc_origin_explainer_what: EMSC (the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre) does not compute locations itself. It collects them from seismological agencies around the world and shows you one of those solutions.
detail_emsc_origin_explainer_how: These figures say who calculated the location shown here and when it was last revised. They do not measure how precise it is.
detail_emsc_author_explain: The agency whose location EMSC is showing, such as NEIC, the USGS National Earthquake Information Center. EMSC aggregates solutions from many agencies, so the same Earthquake can appear with slightly different locations.
detail_emsc_catalog_explain: The EMSC data stream this record came from. For example, EMSC-RTS is the real-time catalog, where Earthquakes appear within minutes and are revised afterward.
detail_emsc_flynn_region_explain: A name from the Flynn–Engdahl regionalization, a standard set of named seismic regions that covers the whole planet. It lets agencies label Earthquakes consistently, wherever they happen.
detail_emsc_last_update_explain: When EMSC last changed this record. Solutions get revised as more stations report in, so the location, depth and magnitude can still shift.
detail_shakemap_source_link: IRIS, P wave vs. S wave (speeds)
detail_felt_legend_cells: Each bubble groups nearby reports: its color is their average Intensity and its size is the number of reports. Zoom in to split the bubbles down to cells of about 10 km.
meaning_footnote: Effects are estimated from Magnitude, Depth and distance with a standard model. Real shaking also depends on the ground and the buildings.
error_source_hint: Its service may be busy. Retry, or switch to {source}.
no_results_hint: Try a wider area or a longer period.
meaning_at_point: Likely Intensity {roman} ({level}) at the selected point
meaning_at_point_not_felt: Likely not felt at the selected point
not_found_body: The page you were looking for doesn't exist or has moved.
error_body: Something went wrong while loading this page. Try again, or go back to the list.
